## 75b8cb3d5e9b

**Status: reproduced teaching-domain gap; audited source left unchanged.** The audited generator is exactly SHA-256 `f9d66697f3d1b36e8f1d1c37d124e1ee410361a9d754743fcd74d38304359143`, with `RULE_HASH = 9c9988768752`.

The generator accepts canonical tie cases but deliberately samples only source/target pairs with one fitting D4 transform. Canonical pair 0 passes both `self_check` and `strict_canonical_like`, yet its source→target relation has two candidates, code 1 (`r1`) and code 6 (`fv`), and those candidates produce different query answers. The canonical Racket authority chooses the first candidate (`r1`); a plausible “choose the last fitting transform” rival chooses `fv` and disagrees. Because every generated training row has exactly one candidate, first-match and last-match policies are observationally identical on the stochastic teaching manifold.

The independent audit census sampled 112 consecutive indices in each of the default/easy/medium/hard bands, using seed `900000 + sample_index`: all **448/448** generated inputs had one candidate and therefore could not teach the accepted precedence rule. This is not a wrong-label finding; it is a mismatch between the accepted legal/canonical domain and what the generator teaches. A repair could either schedule a small number of accepted tie cases whose query distinguishes precedence, with an executable tie-break rival, or explicitly narrow the accepted domain so precedence is not claimed as learned behavior.

Evidence: `checks/audit/75b8cb3d5e9b/probe.json`, `checks/audit/75b8cb3d5e9b/input.json`, `checks/audit/75b8cb3d5e9b/racket.json`, and `checks/audit/75b8cb3d5e9b/rival_output.json`. Reproducer: from `WORK/`, run `PYTHONPATH=repo/shared/runtime:repo python3 checks/audit/75b8cb3d5e9b/audit_probe.py`; the supported Racket command is recorded inside `racket.json`.
